title: YOUR WIFE HASN’T WANTED SEX IN MONTHS. ARE YOU WRONG FOR FEELING REJECTED?
paragraphs: YOUR WIFE HASN’T WANTED SEX IN MONTHS. ARE YOU WRONG FOR FEELING REJECTED?

When the woman you love no longer reaches for you, the silence can break something inside you. But before rejection becomes resentment, there is a truth about marriage, intimacy, and the love of Jesus Christ that both husbands and wives desperately need to hear.
There is a kind of loneliness that only a married person can understand.
It is lying in bed beside someone you promised to love for the rest of your life… and feeling like you are sleeping a thousand miles apart.
Her back is turned.
The lights are off.
The house is quiet.
You reach toward her, hoping for something small. A touch. A kiss. Maybe just the reassurance that she still wants to be close to you.
But she moves away.
“I'm tired.”
And you tell her it's okay.
Because you love her.
Because you don't want to pressure her.
Because you know marriage is supposed to be about more than sex.
But what she doesn't hear is the conversation that begins inside your head after she falls asleep.
Does she still find me attractive?
Did I do something wrong?
Is there someone else?
Am I asking for too much?
Why do I feel so unwanted by the one person who promised to love me?
And perhaps the question that hurts most…
Am I a bad Christian husband for feeling this way?
Brother, I want you to hear something before you read another sentence.
Your desire to be wanted by your wife does not make you selfish. But what you do with the pain of feeling unwanted will reveal something important about the condition of your heart.
And wife, if you're reading this, please don't leave.
This is not an article written to accuse you.
It is not another message telling you that your body belongs to somebody else regardless of what you are carrying emotionally, physically, or spiritually.
This is about both of you.
Two people who may still love each other deeply but have forgotten how to reach each other without causing pain.
And somewhere between his silent rejection and her silent exhaustion, a marriage that once felt alive has begun to feel like a place where both people are merely surviving.
The tragedy is that sometimes neither spouse is the enemy.
They are both wounded.
They just don't know how to tell each other where it hurts.
And if that describes your marriage, please keep reading.
Because what Scripture actually teaches about intimacy is more beautiful, more demanding, and more compassionate than the arguments people often use to defend themselves.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the expression for “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
Basar means flesh.
Echad means one.
Two people becoming one flesh.
Not one person consuming the other.
Not one person's needs erasing the other's humanity.
One flesh.
A covenant union so profound that what happens to one spouse inevitably affects the other.
Sexual intimacy is one expression of that union, but the biblical vision of marriage reaches beyond the bedroom into companionship, faithfulness, tenderness, responsibility, and shared life.
That is why months without physical intimacy can hurt so deeply.
For some husbands, sex is not merely about physical release.
It is one of the ways they experience closeness, acceptance, affection, and the reassurance that their marriage is still alive.
When that connection disappears, the absence can feel personal even when the reason isn't personal at all.
But here is where the story becomes more complicated.
Your wife may not be rejecting you, even when you genuinely feel rejected.
Read that again.
Because those two realities can exist at the same time.
Your pain can be real.
And your interpretation of her pain can still be incomplete.
Perhaps she has been carrying exhaustion that sleep never seems to fix.
Perhaps childbirth changed her body in ways she still struggles to understand.
Perhaps menopause, hormonal changes, chronic pain, medication, depression, anxiety, or another medical concern has affected her desire.
Perhaps physical intimacy has become uncomfortable or painful, and she is embarrassed to tell you.
Perhaps she spends every day caring for children, managing responsibilities, meeting expectations, and trying to remain emotionally available to everyone until she has almost nothing left.
Or perhaps something happened between the two of you.
Something neither of you has fully addressed.
A harsh word.
A betrayal.
A pattern of criticism.
Years of feeling unheard.
An apology that was spoken but never followed by change.
And now, when you reach for her body, she remembers the distance she feels in her heart.
Not every marriage has these problems. Not every woman experiences desire the same way. And not every period without sex means something is broken.
But sometimes what looks like sexual rejection is the visible symptom of a much deeper wound.
And sometimes a husband has been hurting so long that he has stopped asking questions and started making accusations.
He says, “You never want me anymore.”
She hears, “You're failing me again.”
She says, “All you ever think about is sex.”
He hears, “Your need for closeness disgusts me.”
Then both retreat.
He becomes quieter.
She becomes more guarded.
He stops reaching.
She feels relieved that the pressure has stopped, but frightened by the growing distance.
And neither realizes how much love is being buried beneath conversations they are too afraid to have.
This is where many Christian marriages need more than another sermon about marital duty.
They need the truth of God's Word understood in its proper context.
First Corinthians 7:3–4 says:
“Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.” (KJV)
Some people read those verses and immediately conclude that a wife is obligated to have sex whenever her husband desires it.
But notice what Paul actually says.
“And likewise also.”
The Greek text of verse 4 includes the words ὁμοίως δὲ καί — homoiōs de kai, expressing the reciprocal nature of Paul's instruction: “and likewise also.”
Paul does not give the husband unilateral authority while denying the wife equal consideration.
He speaks of mutuality.
The husband is not presented as the sole owner of marital intimacy.
The wife is not presented as someone whose physical or emotional well-being can be disregarded.
Both spouses are called to care for one another.
In verse 5, Paul continues:
“Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again…” (KJV)
The Greek expression ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou means “by agreement” or “by mutual consent.”
That matters.
Paul treats sexual intimacy as an important part of marriage and encourages spouses not to neglect one another. Yet his teaching is framed by reciprocity and agreement, not intimidation or force.
These verses must never become weapons for demanding sex, overriding a spouse's refusal, or excusing coercion.
A biblical understanding of marital intimacy calls both husband and wife toward loving, willing, considerate participation.
It does not turn either person's body into a tool for satisfying the other at any cost.
And if someone has used Scripture to frighten, pressure, or force you into sexual activity, that misuse of Scripture does not reflect Christlike love.
Marriage does not eliminate the need for consent.
Love does not become righteous simply because it quotes a Bible verse.
Now, husband, I need to ask you something that may be uncomfortable.
When was the last time you touched your wife without hoping it would lead somewhere?
When was the last time you held her without turning the embrace into an invitation?
When was the last time you asked how she was doing and stayed long enough to hear the answer she was afraid to give?
Not because you were trying to earn intimacy later.
But because she is your wife.
A human being.
A daughter made in the image of God.
Someone whose heart matters even on the nights when her body cannot give you what you desire.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from agapaō.
Paul commands husbands to love their wives according to the pattern of Christ's self-giving love.
And look at the example.
Jesus gave Himself.
He did not exploit the weakness of those He loved.
He did not use His authority to serve His own comfort.
He sacrificed Himself for their good.
That is the standard Christian husbands are called toward.
Not perfection.
Not pretending they have no needs.
But a love that refuses to make another person's vulnerability an opportunity for selfishness.
Husband, your loneliness deserves to be heard.
But your loneliness does not give you permission to punish your wife.
Not through threats.
Not through humiliation.
Not through comparisons with other women.
Not through pornography, an affair, or emotional withdrawal designed to make her suffer.
And not by using the Bible to make her feel guilty until she gives in.
You can be deeply disappointed without becoming cruel.
You can express your needs without demanding compliance.
You can say, “I miss being close to you,” without saying, “You owe me.”
That difference can change the entire atmosphere of a marriage.
But wife, there is something important for you to hear as well.
Your husband's longing for intimacy is not automatically evidence that he is shallow, lustful, or spiritually immature.
Sometimes he is trying to tell you something he doesn't know how to put into words.
I miss us.
I miss feeling chosen.
I miss knowing that you want to be close to me.
And if you have been turning away because you are exhausted, hurting, afraid, or emotionally disconnected, your experience deserves compassion.
You should never have to endure unwanted sexual activity to prove that you are a faithful wife.
But when it is safe to do so, your husband also deserves an honest conversation rather than endless uncertainty.
Not an obligation to give him sex.
An invitation to help him understand what has changed.
Perhaps the conversation begins with something as simple as:
“I love you. But something has been happening inside me, and I don't fully understand it either.”
Or:
“I want us to be close again, but I need you to understand why intimacy has become difficult.”
And perhaps his response needs to be:
“Thank you for telling me. I don't want you to feel pressured. I want to understand what you're going through, because I miss you, not just sex.”
Can you imagine what might happen if those words replaced months of blame?
Not every wound would disappear overnight.
Some problems require medical care, counseling, repentance, rebuilding trust, or patient changes in daily life.
And some marriages have serious issues of abuse or coercion that require protection and specialized support rather than simply more communication.
But in a marriage where both people are willing and safe, honesty can open a door that resentment has kept closed.
James 1:19 says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.” (KJV)
Sometimes the most spiritual thing a husband can do is stop preparing his defense long enough to understand his wife.
Sometimes the most loving thing a wife can do is stop assuming her husband's pain is merely a complaint about sex and listen to the loneliness underneath it.
And sometimes the most courageous thing both can do is admit:
“We have been hurting each other, and we need help.”
There is no shame in seeking help.

A qualified marriage counselor can help couples communicate about resentment, desire, and emotional distance. A healthcare professional can evaluate pain, hormonal concerns, medication effects, or other possible contributors to changes in sexual desire.
Prayer matters.
So does wise, practical care.
Faith and appropriate treatment are not enemies.
But I want to take you somewhere deeper now.
Because there is a danger in making your spouse's desire the final verdict on your worth.
Husband, if your wife has not wanted sex for months, you may begin to believe that you are no longer desirable, masculine, valuable, or loved.
And if that belief takes root, it can poison more than your marriage.
You may start looking for validation elsewhere.
A compliment from another woman suddenly feels unusually powerful.
A private message becomes tempting.
Pornography begins to look like an escape from rejection.
You tell yourself that you are only trying to feel wanted.
But sin has a way of offering temporary relief while deepening the very loneliness we are trying to escape.
And if you are standing at that crossroads right now, please hear this.
Do not let a season of unmet desire become the doorway to a lifetime of regret.
Your pain matters.
But pain does not make betrayal righteous.
Jesus speaks directly to the heart in Matthew 5:28, warning against looking at another person with lustful intent.
He does not treat private desire as morally insignificant simply because no one else can see it.
That is uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we want God to confront our spouse's failures while leaving our own secret compromises untouched.
We want Him to fix what hurts us without exposing what is corrupting us.
But Christ loves us too much to leave us hiding.
He calls us to repentance.
Not because His grace is small.
Because His grace is powerful enough to lead us out of the darkness.
And this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Jesus did not come merely to make unhappy husbands feel better or exhausted wives feel less guilty.
He came to save sinners.
People whose hearts are capable of selfishness, pride, bitterness, dishonesty, and unfaithfulness.
People who need more than relationship advice.
People who need redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Notice the timing.
While we were still sinners.
Before we had repaired everything.
Before we had learned to love perfectly.
Before we had become the people we should have been.
Christ died for us.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who turn to Him in faith.
That is not permission to continue hurting others.
It is the very reason we can stop pretending, confess our sins, and begin walking in a new direction.
The husband who has been feeding bitterness can repent.
The wife who has been concealing painful truths may find the courage to speak.
The spouse who has betrayed trust can stop hiding and accept responsibility.
The couple who has forgotten how to pray together can begin again.
And the person whose marriage cannot be repaired by their efforts alone can still discover that Christ has not abandoned them.
Because the Gospel is not the promise that every marriage will be restored exactly as we want.
It is the promise that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save, forgive, sustain, and transform those who belong to Him.
Sometimes grace brings reconciliation.
Sometimes it brings the courage to confront destructive patterns.
Sometimes it brings protection, truth, and necessary boundaries.
But grace never requires someone to pretend that harm is love.
And grace never tells a wounded person that their value depends on another human being's sexual desire.
Brother, you were made in God's image before you became somebody's husband.
Sister, you were made in God's image before you became somebody's wife.
Your dignity did not begin on your wedding day.
And it does not disappear in a season of sexual difficulty.
That truth should humble both of you.
Because the person lying beside you is not merely someone who can meet your needs.
That person bears the image of the Creator.
Think about that the next time you are tempted to reduce your spouse to a disappointment.
Think about that the next time you are tempted to dismiss a pain you don't understand.
Think about that when you want to win the argument more than you want to understand the person.
Colossians 3:13 calls believers to forgive one another, just as Christ has forgiven them.
But forgiveness does not erase the need for truth, repentance, safety, or changed behavior.
And reconciliation cannot be manufactured by one spouse while the other refuses accountability.
Christian love is not the denial of reality.
It is the courage to face reality under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
So what do you do tonight?
Maybe your wife is already asleep.
Maybe you have not been intimate in three months.
Six months.
A year.
Maybe you have stopped counting because every passing week feels like another reminder of how far apart you have become.
You don't need to solve everything before sunrise.
You don't need a perfect speech.
But perhaps tomorrow, at a calm moment when neither of you feels pressured, you can say something different.
Not, “Why don't you ever want me?”
But:
“I've been feeling lonely, and I haven't known how to talk about it without making you feel blamed. I miss being close to you. I want to understand what you've been experiencing. Can we talk?”
And then listen.
Really listen.
Even if the answer is difficult.
Even if she says something you didn't expect.
Even if you discover that the problem is not simply a lack of desire, but a wound that needs attention.
And wife, if your husband approaches you with genuine humility, consider meeting that honesty with honesty of your own, if you feel safe.
You do not have to promise sex.
You do not have to manufacture desire.
You can begin with the truth.
“I've been struggling too.”
“I've been afraid to talk about this.”
“I need us to rebuild something.”
Maybe the first step toward intimacy will not be sex.
Maybe it will be a conversation without accusations.
A medical appointment.
A counseling session.
An apology that names the actual harm.
A practical change in how responsibilities are shared.
A hug that carries no hidden expectation.
A prayer spoken through tears.
And perhaps, over time, you will discover that genuine intimacy is not simply the moment two bodies come together.
It is the growing trust that allows two people to be honest, vulnerable, and lovingly present with one another.
The Song of Songs celebrates marital desire as something beautiful, not shameful.
In Song of Solomon 7:10, the bride says:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated “desire” is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
It speaks of longing or desire.
In this poetic context, the bride rejoices in her beloved's desire for her.
There is tenderness in that.
Mutual delight.
The joy of being loved and wanted.
God has not made sexual desire inherently dirty.
But He has also not made sexual desire an excuse to disregard love.
The beauty of marital intimacy is not found in one person winning access to another person's body.
It is found in affection and desire expressed within faithful, loving, mutually willing union.
And that is worth protecting.
Not just the frequency of sex.
The heart of the marriage.
Because a couple can have sex regularly and still be emotionally distant.
And a couple can experience a difficult season without sex while continuing to show extraordinary tenderness, loyalty, and love.
The question is not simply, “How do we get back to having sex?”
It is also, “How do we love each other faithfully in the situation we are facing?”
That question takes us closer to Christ.

And maybe, just maybe, the greatest breakthrough in your marriage will begin when you stop seeing your spouse as the obstacle to your happiness and begin seeing each other as people who need God's grace.
Husband, you are not wrong for feeling rejected.
Feelings of rejection can be painful, even when rejection was not intended.
But do not allow that feeling to become the authority over everything you believe about your wife.
Wife, you are not wrong for experiencing low desire, exhaustion, or difficulty with intimacy.
But when possible and safe, do not let silence become the only language your husband receives.
Neither of you has to pretend.
Neither of you has to surrender your dignity.
Both of you can bring your struggles into the light.
And both of you need Jesus.
Not a Jesus who simply takes your side against your spouse.
The real Jesus.
The One who exposes sin without abandoning the repentant.
The One who welcomes the weary.
The One who teaches us to love with humility and truth.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One who can transform hearts that human effort alone cannot change.
If this article has exposed something in you, don't rush past it.
Maybe you are a husband who has been quietly drowning in rejection.
Maybe you are a wife who feels exhausted by expectations nobody seems to understand.
Maybe you are both.

Or, if you are comfortable sharing, tell us what you wish husbands and wives understood about emotional and physical intimacy. You do not need to disclose private details, and you never have to expose your spouse publicly to receive prayer.
Your words may help another person realize they are not alone.
Not to use as evidence against your spouse.
You may never know which husband is silently questioning his worth or which wife is crying because she cannot explain what has changed inside her.
Because the world is already full of voices teaching people how to defend themselves.
We need more voices reminding people how to follow Jesus.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to glorify a page.
Not to build a personality.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
But I want to be careful here because the Word of God deserves honesty.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the heart of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not the suggestion that you must pay to prove your love for Jesus.
But an opportunity to participate in work you believe is faithfully serving Him.
And beyond the products, the deeper invitation is to stay connected to biblical nourishment, spiritual encouragement, accountability, and discipleship that continually points back to Christ.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value before God.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And no one should ever be made to feel that Christ's love must be purchased.
Before you leave, I want to speak one last time to the husband who began reading this article with a wounded heart.
You may still be lying beside your wife tonight without the physical affection you have been longing for.
The conversation may not happen immediately.
The answers may be more complicated than you hoped.
And the road toward healing may require patience, courage, outside help, and difficult changes from both of you.
But please don't let disappointment turn you into someone you never wanted to become.
Don't surrender your integrity because you feel unseen.
Don't confuse your wife's present lack of sexual desire with a final judgment on your worth.
Don't make your marriage an altar where your spouse must continually prove that you matter.
You matter because God made you.
And the cross of Jesus Christ reveals a love far greater than any human relationship can provide.
To the wife who has been carrying a burden she cannot explain, you are seen too.
Your exhaustion matters.
Your pain matters.
Your voice matters.
You are not simply a body that must perform to preserve somebody else's confidence.
You are a person worthy of dignity, tenderness, and truth.
And to both of you…
Perhaps tonight you can begin with a simple prayer.

“Lord Jesus, forgive us for the ways we have allowed fear, selfishness, bitterness, or silence to shape our marriage. Help us see each other with compassion. Give us courage to speak honestly, humility to listen, wisdom to seek help where needed, and strength to repent wherever we have sinned. Protect us from temptation and teach us to love in ways that honor You. Whether healing comes quickly or slowly, keep our hearts anchored in Your truth. In Your name, amen.”
Your marriage may be in a painful chapter.
But your story is not beyond the reach of God's grace.
And even if the outcome is different from what you prayed for, your life is still held by the risen Savior.
Because sometimes the deepest wound in a marriage is not that two people have stopped touching.
It is that two hearts have been crying out to be loved, while neither has known how to hear the other.
